title: Create Your Offer
lede: Use these four prompts in order to finish your offer with Jarvis.
body:
Keep this in the same Jarvis project with your skill pack loaded. Jarvis uses your earlier answers, researches the service and writes the offer. You choose what to keep.

Start with who you can understand and reach.

Choose who you want to help

Start with a business you know or can reach. If you already picked a service, tell Jarvis and find the buyer who needs it. If you have no experience, say that. Jarvis should ask about your interests, access and location before recommending options.

You: “I worked in a roofing office. I want to work with residential roofers in Dallas.”

Choice: Residential roofing company owners in Dallas. That is who the rest of the example is about.

Use the offer menu skill to help me choose one niche from my background, interests and any service I already have in mind. Ask what you need, then save my chosen buyer and location.

Before continuing: answer Jarvis’s questions and choose one buyer. Don’t move on with a list of five niches.

Use that buyer to choose one problem and service.

Find a problem they would pay to solve

Now Jarvis researches that buyer and matches a useful service to the problem. You can use the service examples, an offer found elsewhere or deeper custom research.

Problem to investigate: The roofer has unsold estimates but no consistent follow-up.

Service: Follow up eligible estimates and bring interested homeowners back to the sales team.

Why it matters: They already spent time winning the enquiry and preparing the quote.

Use the offer menu skill to research my chosen buyer, recommend one worthwhile problem and service with real examples. Show how to estimate what the problem costs using the owner’s numbers, and explain what I need to confirm with owners.

Before continuing: choose the problem you can explain. Public research gives you a starting point; owner conversations check whether it is real for them.

Know the delivery behind the promise.

Know what the service actually does

Get clear on the workflow and delivery before you promise a result.

The roofing service: Find eligible unsold estimates, send approved follow-up, handle agreed questions and pass interested homeowners to the sales rep. The rep still answers technical questions, closes and delivers the roofing job.

Check before selling: access to the CRM, the usable pipeline, the delivery cost and whether your team or developer can build it.

Use the offer menu skill and my saved decisions to explain the problem, workflow, client responsibilities and delivery route in plain language. Save the service brief and flag the facts we must check before promising a result.

Before continuing: explain the service in two sentences. Take technical gaps to your developer or technical CSM.

Turn the saved service brief into the six lines.

Turn that service into the offer

The offer creation skill now uses the saved brief. You should not need to explain the whole business again.

Niche: Residential roofers in Dallas with eligible unsold estimates.
Outcome: Five more paid roofing jobs.
Timeframe: Within 30 days of campaign launch.
Risk reversal: Work free until the agreed target is reached.
Authority / proof: A working demonstration of the follow-up workflow.
Unique mechanism: The Estimate Recovery System.

Use my saved service brief and the offer creation skill to write my six lines. Reuse my decisions and mark anything we still need to confirm.

Before continuing: make sure the offer matches the service you understand and can deliver. Ask Jarvis to save the chosen version.

Then build your landing page from that same offer. The headline sells the result; the subheadline explains how.
